title: Deadlocks and classic synchronisation problems
scopeHtml:
Scope: Coffman conditions, prevention, avoidance, detection, producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers and real hangs.

Scope: Coffman conditions, prevention, avoidance, detection, producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers and real hangs.

notes.title: What a deadlock is
notes.html:
A deadlock is when a group of threads each wait for something another in the group holds, so none can ever move. No crash, no error, no CPU use. The service just stops answering and thread count climbs.

Smallest example: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.

// Thread 1                          // Thread 2
synchronized (a) {                   synchronized (b) {
    synchronized (b) { ... }             synchronized (a) { ... }
}                                    }

Worked example. A transfer function locks the source account then the destination. Alice sends to Bob while Bob sends to Alice at the same moment: T1 locks Alice, T2 locks Bob, T1 waits for Bob, T2 waits for Alice. With 5,000 transfers/s over 1 million accounts, the chance that two opposite transfers overlap is small but not zero, so it fires once a week in production, usually at peak.

How to see it in production.

$ jstack 2310
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-12":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f2c (object 0x000000076ab1, a Account),
  which is held by "transfer-7"
"transfer-7":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f2d (object 0x000000076ab2, a Account),
  which is held by "transfer-12"

For native programs: gdb -p PID -batch -ex "thread apply all bt" and look for many threads in __lll_lock_wait / futex_wait. Symptoms in metrics: throughput drops to zero while CPU is near idle, thread pool queue grows, health check times out.

Industry examples. MySQL InnoDB and Postgres detect row-lock deadlocks and kill one transaction (ERROR 1213 Deadlock found / deadlock detected), so apps must retry. Java's ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() is used by monitoring agents.

Everyday analogy. Two cars meet on a single-lane bridge, each waiting for the other to back up.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up deadlock (waiting forever, no CPU) with livelock (running but making no progress) and starvation (one thread never gets served).
  • Thinking a deadlock needs locks only. It can involve semaphores, DB rows, file locks, or a thread pool waiting on its own queue.

notes.title: The four Coffman conditions
notes.html:
A deadlock can happen only if all four conditions hold at once. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. Coffman listed them in 1971.

  1. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away by force; the holder must release it.
  4. Circular wait: a cycle exists: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T3, ..., Tn waits for T1.
Condition How to break it Cost
Mutual exclusion Make the resource shareable (read-only data, lock-free, immutable) Not always possible (a printer, a row being updated)
Hold and wait Take all locks at once, or release everything before waiting Lower concurrency, risk of starvation
No preemption Use tryLock with timeout and back off (give up what you hold) Need retry logic; livelock risk
Circular wait Global lock ordering Needs discipline across the codebase; cheapest

Worked example (the resource-allocation graph). Draw threads as circles and resources as squares. Edge R -> T means T holds R; edge T -> R means T waits for R. With one instance of each resource, a cycle in the graph means deadlock. With several instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

Decision gravity. In practice 95% of deadlocks are fixed by breaking circular wait with an ordering rule, because it is free at runtime and easy to review. Hold-and-wait removal hurts throughput. Preemption works for databases (abort a transaction, roll back) but is hard for in-memory locks.

Everyday analogy. Four cars at a crossroads each waiting for the car on their right: all four conditions hold (road space is exclusive, each holds its spot while wanting the next, nobody can be pushed, and they form a circle).

Common interview traps.

  • Listing the conditions but not saying "all four needed, so removing one is enough".
  • Claiming a cycle always means deadlock; with multiple resource instances it may not.

notes.title: Prevention
notes.html:
Prevention means designing the code so that at least one Coffman condition can never hold. It costs nothing at runtime if done by convention, so it is the first line of defence.

1. Lock ordering (breaks circular wait). Give every lock a rank; always acquire in increasing rank. For transfers, order by account id.

void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    Account first  = from.id < to.id ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id < to.id ? to   : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
        }
    }
}

2. Try-lock with timeout (breaks no-preemption and hold-and-wait).

if (a.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
  try {
    if (b.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
      try { work(); } finally { b.unlock(); }
    } else { /* back off: release a, sleep random 1-20 ms, retry */ }
  } finally { a.unlock(); }
}

Add random back-off or two threads retrying in lock-step produce a livelock.

3. Acquire everything up front, or use one coarse lock. Simplest and often right below a few thousand ops/s.

4. Do not call unknown code while holding a lock (callbacks, listeners, Object.equals of user types). The hidden callee may take another lock in the opposite order.

Linux kernel practice. The kernel documents lock order in comments and uses lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) to learn the acquisition graph at runtime and warn about potential cycles before they ever deadlock. Output looks like WARNING: possible circular locking dependency detected. In user space, Clang's thread-safety annotations and TSan's deadlock detector do similar checks.

Industry examples. Postgres orders buffer-lock acquisition rules; MySQL advises to access tables and rows in the same order in every transaction. Go has no lockdep, so teams use go-deadlock in tests.

Everyday analogy. Numbering all tools in a shared workshop and agreeing "always pick up the lower number first": no two people can ever each hold what the other needs.

Common interview traps.

  • Ordering by memory address works but hides intent; ordering by stable id is clearer. Not handling from == to (locking the same object twice) is a real bug.
  • Using tryLock without back-off or a retry limit.
  • Thinking Java synchronized can time out. It cannot; use ReentrantLock.tryLock.

notes.title: Avoidance and the Banker's algorithm
notes.html:
Avoidance means the system grants a request only if it keeps the state "safe", meaning some order exists in which every thread can finish. It needs to know each thread's maximum future needs in advance.

Banker's algorithm (Dijkstra). Think of a bank with limited cash and customers with credit limits. Before lending, check: after this loan, could the bank still pay out so everyone eventually finishes? If yes, the state is safe and the loan is granted; if not, the borrower waits.

Worked example. 12 units of one resource. Maximum needs and current holdings: P1 max 10 holds 5, P2 max 4 holds 2, P3 max 9 holds 2. Free = 12 - 9 = 3.

  • P2 needs 2 more; 3 free, so P2 finishes and returns 4, so free becomes 3 - 2 + 4 = 5.
  • P1 needs 5 more; free is 5, so P1 finishes and returns 10. Free = 10.
  • P3 needs 7 more; free is 10, so it finishes. Safe sequence: P2, P1, P3. If P3 had asked for 1 more earlier and the system had only left 2 free, no sequence might exist and the request would be delayed.

Why almost no real OS uses it. It needs advance maximum claims (applications do not know them), a fixed number of threads, and the check is O(m x n^2). Real systems prefer prevention by ordering, or detection and recovery. Avoidance does appear in embedded and real-time systems with static task sets, and in a lighter form: admission control (limit the number of transactions or connections so resources cannot be exhausted).

Decision gravity. Avoidance is conservative (it refuses some safe requests, lowering utilisation) and complex; prevention and detection are chosen in practice. Reversible but rarely worth it.

Everyday analogy. A bank manager who refuses a loan if it would leave no money for the remaining customers to ever complete their projects.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing a safe state with "no deadlock right now". An unsafe state may still not deadlock; it just can.
  • Saying Linux uses the Banker's algorithm. It does not.

notes.title: Detection and recovery
notes.html:
Detection lets deadlocks happen, finds them, and breaks them. It suits systems where deadlocks are rare and a victim can be rolled back, mainly databases.

How to detect. Keep a wait-for graph: node per transaction, edge T1 -> T2 if T1 waits for a lock T2 holds. A cycle is a deadlock. Run a cycle search (depth-first) periodically or when a wait exceeds a threshold.

How to recover.

  1. Kill a victim: pick by cheapest rollback (fewest rows changed, youngest, lowest priority), abort it, release its locks.
  2. Preempt and roll back to a savepoint.
  3. Avoid starvation: do not always choose the same victim; count how many times a transaction was picked.

Real databases.

  • InnoDB: checks the wait-for graph immediately on lock wait (innodb_deadlock_detect=ON by default). Picks the transaction with the least changed rows. With very hot rows, detection itself becomes costly (many waiters); some set innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s; lower it).
  • PostgreSQL: waits deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) before running detection, then aborts one with ERROR: deadlock detected and shows both statements in the log.
mysql> SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
------------------------
LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
------------------------
*** (1) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-10 WHERE id=1
*** (2) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal+10 WHERE id=2
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)

The app must catch the error and retry the whole transaction (usually 3 attempts with jitter).

In-process detection. JVM: jstack or ThreadMXBean. Watchdog thread that timestamps lock waits and dumps stacks after 10 s. Kubernetes liveness probes will restart a deadlocked pod after e.g. 3 failed checks, which hides the bug: always capture a thread dump before the restart.

Industry examples. Oracle and SQL Server also kill victims (SQL Server error 1205). Google Spanner uses wound-wait to avoid deadlocks: an older transaction "wounds" (aborts) a younger one that holds a needed lock, and a younger one waits for an older one.

Everyday analogy. A traffic marshal who spots a gridlocked junction and orders one car to reverse out.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the application retry. The DB aborting is normal behaviour, not a bug in the DB.
  • Not mentioning that detection costs CPU and can itself be a bottleneck under heavy contention.

notes.title: Producer-consumer
notes.html:
Producers create items, consumers process them; a bounded buffer sits in between so the two sides run at different speeds. Producers must wait when the buffer is full, consumers must wait when it is empty, and access to the buffer must be exclusive.

Classic solution with three semaphores: empty (starts at N, free slots), full (starts at 0, filled slots), and mutex (1, protects the buffer).

producer:                   consumer:
  wait(empty)                 wait(full)
  wait(mutex)                 wait(mutex)
  buffer.put(item)            item = buffer.take()
  signal(mutex)               signal(mutex)
  signal(full)                signal(empty)

Swap the first two waits in either side (take mutex before empty/full) and you get a deadlock: a producer holds the mutex while sleeping on empty, consumers can never get the mutex to free a slot.

BlockingQueue<Job> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);
// producer: q.put(job);    blocks when full  (back-pressure)
// consumer: Job j = q.take(); blocks when empty

Worked example. Producers make 5,000 jobs/s, consumers process 3,000 jobs/s. An unbounded queue grows 2,000 jobs/s: at 1 KB each that is 2 MB/s, so 7 GB per hour until OOM. A bounded queue of 1,000 forces producers to block (back-pressure), and the speed mismatch becomes visible instead of fatal. Choosing the bound: about (peak burst length x rate difference). Alternatives when blocking is unacceptable: drop, shed load with 429, or spill to disk/Kafka.

Industry examples. Kafka is a durable distributed producer-consumer log. Java ThreadPoolExecutor has a work queue; Go channels (make(chan Job, 1000)) are bounded queues; Linux pipes are 64 KB kernel buffers (the writer blocks when full).

Everyday analogy. A kitchen pass: chefs put plates on a shelf with 10 spots, waiters take them. A full shelf stops the chefs; an empty one makes the waiters wait.

Common interview traps.

  • Unbounded queues. They hide overload until memory is gone; always state the bound and the full-queue policy.
  • Wrong semaphore order. Say why it deadlocks.
  • Not handling shutdown: use a poison-pill item or close the channel so consumers exit.

notes.title: Readers-writers
notes.html:
Many readers can read together; a writer needs exclusive access. It is common (config, caches, routing tables). The problem is policy: who wins when both wait?

  • Readers-preference: new readers join while a reader is active. High read throughput, but a steady stream of readers starves writers.
  • Writers-preference: once a writer waits, new readers queue behind it. Fixes writer starvation, may slow readers.
  • Fair (FIFO): requests served in arrival order. Predictable, less parallel.
ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true /* fair */);
String get(String k) { rw.readLock().lock();  try { return m.get(k); }  finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } }
void   put(String k, String v) { rw.writeLock().lock(); try { m.put(k, v); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } }

Worked example. A read takes 1 microsecond and a write 100 microseconds; 1,000 reads/s per thread across 16 threads and 10 writes/s. A plain mutex serialises all reads; the RW lock lets 16 readers run together. But the RW lock itself is a shared counter: every readLock is an atomic update on one cache line, so on many cores the readers still bounce that line. The read path then costs 50 to 200 ns instead of 20 ns.

Better options for read-mostly data.

  • Copy-on-write: writer builds a new copy and swaps one pointer atomically (CopyOnWriteArrayList, Go atomic.Value). Readers take no lock at all. Fine when writes are rare and data is small.
  • RCU (read-copy-update): the Linux kernel's way; readers run lock-free, the writer publishes a new version and frees the old after all readers have passed a grace period. Used for routing tables, dentry lookup.
  • Java StampedLock with optimistic reads: read, then validate no write happened; retry if so.
  • Sharding: ConcurrentHashMap.

Decision gravity. RW locks are often not worth it: if writes exceed roughly 10% of operations or critical sections are tiny, a plain mutex wins. Reversible if abstracted.

Everyday analogy. A library reading room: many people read the same notice board at once, but to repaint it everyone must leave.

Common interview traps.

  • Upgrading a read lock to a write lock while holding it: deadlocks in ReentrantReadWriteLock (it does not support upgrade). Release and reacquire, then re-check.
  • Not naming the starvation trade-off.
  • Assuming RW locks are always faster than mutexes.

notes.title: Dining philosophers
notes.html:
Five philosophers sit at a round table, one fork between each pair; to eat, a philosopher needs both adjacent forks. It is the textbook model for deadlock and starvation among threads sharing overlapping resources.

Naive: everyone picks up the left fork, then the right. If all five pick up their left fork at the same time, each waits forever for the right one. All four Coffman conditions hold.

Solutions, each breaking a condition:

  1. Resource ordering (break circular wait): number the forks 0 to 4; always pick the lower-numbered fork first. The last philosopher (forks 4 and 0) picks 0 first, so the cycle cannot close. Simple and starvation-light.
  2. Limit to N-1 diners with a counting semaphore of 4: at least one philosopher can always get both forks.
  3. Waiter / arbitrator (single mutex): ask a waiter for permission to take both forks at once (breaks hold-and-wait). Reduces parallelism.
  4. Chandy-Misra: forks are "clean" or "dirty" and passed by request; decentralised and starvation-free (used in distributed settings).
  5. Try-lock and back off: pick left, try right with timeout, put left down if it fails. Risk of livelock without randomisation.
// Solution 1: order by fork id
int a = Math.min(left, right), b = Math.max(left, right);
forks[a].lock(); forks[b].lock();
try { eat(); } finally { forks[b].unlock(); forks[a].unlock(); }

Worked example. 5 philosophers, eat time 10 ms, think time 10 ms. Max parallel eaters is 2 (5 forks / 2 per eater, floor). Ordering gives about 2 concurrent eaters most of the time; the "N-1 diners" semaphore also reaches 2; the single-waiter solution gives 1. So throughput rank: ordering ~ semaphore > waiter.

Real-world mapping. A thread needing two locks (transfer between accounts), a database transaction updating two rows, or a worker needing two connections from two pools. The solution is always: global order, or take both together.

Everyday analogy. Five people at a table sharing chopsticks: if everyone grabs the left stick, all starve politely.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering "the philosopher waits a random time" as a fix without noting it does not guarantee progress.
  • Forgetting starvation: ordering prevents deadlock, but a fast philosopher may still repeatedly beat a slow neighbour; fairness needs a queue.

notes.title: Other hangs that look like deadlocks
notes.html:
Real incidents are rarely two locks in opposite order. Know these patterns.

  1. Thread pool starvation (self-deadlock). A task running in a pool of 10 threads submits a subtask to the same pool and blocks on its result. If all 10 threads do this, no thread is free to run the subtasks. Fix: separate pools, async composition, or ForkJoinPool which lets a waiting thread help (work stealing).
  2. Lock held across I/O. A thread holds a mutex while calling a slow network service; everyone else stalls for the timeout. Looks like a hang, is really unbounded latency.
  3. Fork and locks. fork() in a multithreaded process copies only the calling thread; if another thread held a lock (even inside malloc), the child's copy of that lock is held forever. Fix: execve right after fork, or use pthread_atfork handlers.
  4. Signal handlers. Calling non-async-signal-safe functions (printf, malloc) inside a handler can self-deadlock on the lock the interrupted code held.
  5. Distributed deadlock. Service A waits for B, B waits for C, C waits for A with synchronous calls and request timeouts of 30 s. Everything times out together; retries amplify the storm. Fix: timeouts decreasing down the chain, circuit breakers, no cyclic call graphs.
  6. Database plus app lock. App takes a Java lock then opens a transaction; another path opens the transaction then takes the lock. Neither the DB nor the JVM sees the cycle, so no detector fires.
  7. Priority inversion (see the concurrency basics note) can look like a hang for the high-priority thread.
$ jstack 2310 | grep -c "pool-1-thread"        # all 10 present
$ jstack 2310 | grep -A4 "pool-1-thread-3"
  java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
    at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(FutureTask.java:191)
    at com.shop.PriceService.compute(PriceService.java:57)

All workers sitting in FutureTask.get is the fingerprint.

Industry examples. Public postmortems frequently cite exhausted connection pools or thread pools with retries creating a metastable failure; Netflix's bulkhead and timeout guidance addresses exactly this.

Everyday analogy. A manager who hires an assistant and then waits for the assistant's report, but the assistant is stuck in a queue behind other managers.

Common interview traps.

  • Restarting the pod and moving on, without taking a thread dump first.
  • Only knowing the "two locks" story; interviewers love the thread-pool self-deadlock.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Deadlock = group waiting in a cycle forever; no CPU use, no error. Find it with jstack, gdb thread dumps, DB deadlock logs.
  • Four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one.
  • Prevention by lock ordering is cheapest and most common; tryLock with timeout and jittered back-off is the second tool; lockdep and TSan find lock-order bugs before production.
  • Avoidance (Banker's algorithm) keeps the system in a safe state but needs advance maximum claims; real systems rarely use it.
  • Detection plus recovery (wait-for graph, kill a victim, retry) is how databases work; apps must retry on deadlock errors.
  • Producer-consumer: bounded buffer with empty, full and mutex semaphores or a blocking queue; bounds give back-pressure.
  • Readers-writers: choose a starvation policy; consider copy-on-write or RCU for read-mostly data.
  • Dining philosophers: order the forks, limit diners to N-1, or use an arbitrator.
  • Many production hangs are pool starvation, locks held over I/O, fork with locks, or cyclic service calls, not classic two-lock deadlocks.

questions.promptHtml: What is a deadlock, and what four conditions must hold for it to occur?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The conditions are the vocabulary for every prevention strategy; naming them shows you can reason, not recite.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for something another in the set holds, so none can ever proceed; no crash, no CPU, just a stopped service. It needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Because all four are needed, breaking any one makes deadlock impossible. In practice breaking circular wait with a global lock order is cheapest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
T1 holds L1, wants L2     T2 holds L2, wants L1     -> cycle
Condition Break it by Cost
Mutual exclusion Immutable/shared/lock-free data Not always possible
Hold and wait Take all locks at once, or release before waiting Lower concurrency
No preemption tryLock with timeout and back off Retry logic, livelock risk
Circular wait Global lock ordering Discipline

Resource-allocation graph: an edge R to T means T holds R; T to R means T waits. With one instance per resource a cycle means deadlock; with multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Thread 1                      // Thread 2
synchronized (a) {               synchronized (b) {
    synchronized (b) { ... }         synchronized (a) { ... }
}                                }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Listing the conditions without saying "all four needed, so removing one is enough".
  • Claiming any cycle is a deadlock; with several instances it may not be.
  • Thinking only locks deadlock; semaphores, DB rows, file locks and thread pools can too.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which condition is easiest to break? -> Circular wait, by ordering locks.
  2. Can a deadlock exist with one lock? -> Yes: non-reentrant relock by the same thread, or a pool waiting on itself.
  3. How do you see it in a JVM? -> jstack prints "Found one Java-level deadlock"; ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The senior ties each condition to a concrete engineering fix and its cost, and notes that 95% of cases are cured by ordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A money-transfer endpoint locked source then destination; opposite transfers froze the service weekly at peak.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between deadlock, livelock and starvation, and how does each look in monitoring?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production hangs get misdiagnosed constantly; the distinction decides which tool you reach for.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Deadlock: threads wait forever for each other, so CPU is near zero and throughput hits zero. Livelock: threads keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress, so CPU is high and work done is zero. Starvation: the system makes progress overall but one thread (or class of work) never gets served, for example writers behind endless readers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CPU Progress Typical cause
Deadlock idle none cyclic wait
Livelock high none tryLock/back-off in lock-step, retry storms
Starvation normal partial unfair lock, readers-preference, priority

Livelock example: two threads both tryLock A then B, fail, release, and retry at the same instant forever; fix with randomised back-off. Starvation fix: fair queues, aging, bounded waiting (the third mutual-exclusion property).

Metrics: deadlock = flat throughput, growing queue, idle CPU, thread dump shows WAITING/BLOCKED in a cycle. Livelock = high CPU with flat throughput, stacks look "busy" in retry loops.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
while (true) {
    if (a.tryLock()) {
        try { if (b.tryLock()) { try { work(); return; } finally { b.unlock(); } } }
        finally { a.unlock(); }
    }
    Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 20));   // jitter breaks the lock-step
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling a retry storm a deadlock.
  • tryLock retry without jitter or a retry limit.
  • Forgetting starvation exists once deadlock is fixed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you tell livelock from a busy-but-healthy service? -> Compare work-done counters with CPU; sample stacks twice.
  2. How do you prevent starvation? -> Fair locks, FIFO queues, aging.
  3. Is a retry storm a livelock? -> A distributed form of it, yes, often with positive feedback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior connects each failure to a metric signature and a remedy, rather than defining three words.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Services with aggressive client retries livelocked their own backend: CPU at 100%, goodput at zero until retries were jittered and capped.

questions.promptHtml: How does a global lock ordering prevent deadlock, and how would you apply it to a two-account transfer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the standard answer; the detail (stable key, same-object case) shows real experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If every thread acquires locks in the same global order, a cycle cannot form, so circular wait is impossible. For a transfer I lock the account with the lower id first, then the higher, and I handle the from == to case separately so I never lock the same object twice. Keep critical sections short and never call unknown code while holding the lock.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
transfer(A,B): lock min(idA,idB) -> lock max -> move money -> unlock both

A cycle needs some thread to hold a higher-ranked lock while waiting for a lower one; the rule forbids it. Order by a stable id, not memory address (clearer, survives moves). Locks acquired in loops or from callbacks are the hard part: document the rank order, and in the Linux kernel enable lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) which learns the acquisition graph and warns "possible circular locking dependency" before a real deadlock. In user space use TSan's deadlock detector or clang thread-safety annotations.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, long amt) {
    if (&from == &to) return;
    std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m);       // acquires both with deadlock avoidance
    from.bal -= amt; to.bal += amt;
}
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    if (from == to) return;
    Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to, second = first == from ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.bal -= amt; to.bal += amt; } }
}
fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, amt: Long) {
    if (from === to) return
    val (first, second) = if (from.id < to.id) from to to else to to from
    synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.bal -= amt; to.bal += amt } }
}
def transfer(frm, to, amt):
    if frm is to: return
    first, second = sorted((frm, to), key=lambda a: a.id)
    with first.lock, second.lock:
        frm.bal -= amt; to.bal += amt

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting from == to (self-lock or double-lock).
  • Ordering by something that can change.
  • Calling callbacks or listeners under the lock, which may take locks out of order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if you need three or more locks? -> Sort them all by rank; std::scoped_lock does this for you.
  2. What if the second lock is only discovered after reading data? -> Release, re-acquire in order and revalidate, or use a coarser lock.
  3. Does ordering prevent starvation? -> No, only deadlock.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior includes the self-transfer edge case, lockdep/TSan enforcement, and a cross-codebase rank document.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: MySQL guidance is "access tables and rows in the same order in every transaction"; same principle, same payoff.

questions.promptHtml: What is a safe state, how does the Banker's algorithm use it, and why does almost no real system use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of avoidance versus prevention versus detection, and practical judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A state is safe if some order exists in which every thread can get its remaining maximum need and finish. The Banker's algorithm pretends to grant a request and grants it only if a safe sequence still exists. It needs each thread's maximum claim in advance, a fixed thread set, and costs O(m x n^2), so real systems use lock ordering, detection and retry, or admission control instead. An unsafe state does not mean deadlock now, just that one is possible.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
12 units total. Max/holding: P1 10/5, P2 4/2, P3 9/2. Free = 12 - 9 = 3.

  • P2 needs 2 and 3 are free, so it finishes and returns 4: free = 5.
  • P1 needs 5 and free is 5, so it finishes and returns 10: free = 10.
  • P3 needs 7 and finishes. Safe sequence P2, P1, P3.

Avoidance is conservative: it refuses some requests that would have been fine, lowering utilisation. Used where task sets are static (embedded, real-time) and as admission control (cap transactions or connections so resources can't be exhausted).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def is_safe(avail, alloc, need):
    work, done = avail[:], [False]*len(alloc)
    progressed = True
    while progressed:
        progressed = False
        for i, n in enumerate(need):
            if not done[i] and all(n[j] <= work[j] for j in range(len(work))):
                work = [work[j] + alloc[i][j] for j in range(len(work))]
                done[i] = progressed = True
    return all(done)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing "unsafe" with "deadlocked".
  • Saying Linux uses it. It does not.
  • Forgetting the need for maximum claims up front.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use it in a database? -> Transactions do not know their lock set in advance; databases detect and abort instead.
  2. What is admission control? -> A lightweight avoidance: limit concurrent users of a pool so the total demand cannot exceed capacity.
  3. Prevention vs avoidance? -> Prevention removes a condition by design; avoidance checks each request dynamically.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states why it is impractical and names what is used instead (ordering, detection plus retry, admission control).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Limiting a service to N in-flight requests per pool of N connections is Banker-lite and prevents pool-exhaustion deadlocks.

questions.promptHtml: How do databases detect and recover from deadlocks, and what must the application do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Backend engineers meet this daily (MySQL 1213, Postgres 40P01); the app-side retry is the real test.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The DB keeps a wait-for graph: a node per transaction, an edge when one waits for a lock another holds. A cycle is a deadlock. It picks a victim (usually the cheapest to roll back), aborts it and releases its locks. The application must catch the deadlock error and retry the whole transaction, typically 3 attempts with jitter. This is normal behaviour, not a DB bug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: InnoDB checks the graph as soon as a lock wait starts (innodb_deadlock_detect=ON), choosing the transaction with fewest changed rows. On extremely hot rows detection itself burns CPU with many waiters; some teams disable it and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s, lower it). PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout (1 s) first and then runs detection, aborting one with ERROR: deadlock detected. SQL Server error 1205, Oracle ORA-00060. Google Spanner avoids cycles with wound-wait: older transactions abort younger lock holders. Victim choice must avoid starving the same transaction.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def run_tx(fn, attempts=3):
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            with db.begin(): return fn()
        except DeadlockError:
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.05 * 2**i))     # jittered back-off
    raise
-- InnoDB: see the latest detected deadlock
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not retrying the transaction, so users see 500s.
  • Retrying only the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
  • Ignoring that detection can be a bottleneck under heavy contention.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How reduce deadlocks? -> Same row access order, short transactions, proper indexes (fewer gap locks).
  2. Why can missing an index cause deadlocks? -> More rows locked, wider lock footprints.
  3. Wait-die vs wound-wait? -> Both use timestamps: wait-die lets old wait for young and kills young requesters; wound-wait lets old abort young holders.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions victim selection, retry with jitter and idempotency, and detection cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flash sale produced hundreds of 1213 errors; shortening transactions and ordering updates by item id removed them.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through the dining philosophers problem, three ways to solve it, and what each costs. Where does it show up in real systems?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a model for any task needing two overlapping resources; interviewers check you map the solution to a real design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Five philosophers, five forks, each needs both adjacent forks. If all grab the left fork, all wait for the right one: deadlock with all four Coffman conditions. Fixes: order the forks and always take the lower number first (breaks circular wait), allow at most four diners with a semaphore (some philosopher can always eat), or use a single waiter that grants both forks together (breaks hold-and-wait but serialises). In real systems it is a thread that needs two locks, or a transaction updating two rows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Max eaters = floor(5/2) = 2. Ordering and the N-1 semaphore both reach about 2 concurrent eaters; the waiter gives 1. Try-lock with back-off works but risks livelock without randomisation. Chandy-Misra (clean/dirty forks passed by request) is decentralised and starvation-free. Note ordering prevents deadlock but not starvation: a fast neighbour can repeatedly win; a queue adds fairness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
int a = Math.min(left, right), b = Math.max(left, right);
forks[a].lock(); forks[b].lock();
try { eat(); } finally { forks[b].unlock(); forks[a].unlock(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Wait a random time" as a guaranteed fix.
  • Forgetting starvation.
  • Not mapping to real life (two locks, two pools).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which has best throughput? -> Ordering and N-1 diners; waiter lowest.
  2. How do you map it to connection pools? -> A request needing connections from two pools acquires in a fixed pool order.
  3. Is the semaphore-of-N-1 deadlock free? -> Yes, with 4 diners the pigeonhole principle leaves one with both forks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior compares solutions by Coffman condition and throughput, and mentions fairness.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A worker needing a DB connection and a downstream HTTP slot from separate pools deadlocked until both were acquired in one fixed order.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate implements a bounded buffer with semaphores empty = N, full = 0, mutex = 1. Under load the process hangs: 100% of threads idle, queue length constant at N.

def producer(item):
    mutex.acquire()          # line 1
    empty.acquire()          # line 2
    buf.append(item)
    mutex.release()
    full.release()

def consumer():
    full.acquire()
    mutex.acquire()
    item = buf.pop(0)
    mutex.release()
    empty.release()
    return item

Thread dump shows: one producer blocked in empty.acquire() while holding mutex; 8 consumers blocked in mutex.acquire().
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it only appears when the buffer fills, and fix it. What else would you check?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase N." That just delays the hang.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single or multiple producers? Is shutdown handled? Is a library queue allowed? Do we need back-pressure or drop?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart with a thread dump saved; meanwhile switch to queue.Queue(maxsize=N).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) producer takes mutex before empty: lock held while sleeping; (b) missing release on exception; (c) consumer ordering also wrong; (d) lost semaphore signal. The dump confirms (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Dump shows who holds mutex (the sleeping producer); a test with N=1 hangs immediately.
  5. Root cause: When the buffer is full the producer holds mutex and sleeps on empty. Consumers need mutex to remove an item and eventually release empty, so nobody can move: hold-and-wait with a circular dependency.
  6. Fix: Acquire the counting semaphore first, the mutex second, release in reverse, and use try/finally.
def producer(item):
    empty.acquire()
    with mutex: buf.append(item)
    full.release()

Long-term: queue.Queue(maxsize=N) or BlockingQueue. 7. Prevention: Test with N=1 and 1 producer; review rule "acquire counters before mutex"; use library queues. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the queue unbounded to avoid the full case; that hides overload until OOM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you shut down consumers? -> Poison pill per consumer or a closed flag checked with full released.
  • Is the consumer order the same bug? -> Same: take full then mutex.
  • Why does it hang only at full? -> Only then does the producer sleep inside the mutex.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A job runner passed all tests with a buffer of 1000 and deadlocked the first time a backlog filled it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises N or adds timeouts.
  • Hire: swaps order and explains why.
  • Strong hire: N=1 test, shutdown design, prefers library queue with back-pressure policy.

questions.contextHtml:
After "fixing" deadlocks with ordering, the transfer service still freezes about twice a month, and sometimes a thread hangs alone.

void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    Account first  = from.id < to.id ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id < to.id ? to   : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(amt);            // calls listener.onChange(from)
            to.credit(amt);
        }
    }
}
// elsewhere
void audit(Account a) { synchronized (auditLock) { synchronized (a) { ... } } }
// AccountListener.onChange() { synchronized (auditLock) { log(...); } }

jstack shows a cycle between a transfer thread (holds account, wants auditLock) and an audit thread (holds auditLock, wants account). One hung thread has from == to.
questions.promptHtml: What are the two or three remaining bugs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The ordering is correct, so it must be the JVM." Misses the listener callback and the self-transfer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is auditLock ordered relative to accounts anywhere? What does a listener do? How is from == to handled upstream?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the audit path or listener temporarily; reject from == to at the API.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock-order inversion with auditLock via the callback; (b) from == to relocks the same monitor (reentrant, so only a logic bug, but with ReentrantLock pairs or non-reentrant locks it hangs); (c) a different path locks accounts out of id order; (d) Integer id comparison with ==.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack cycle shown; grep all synchronized blocks for lock sequences; test with self-transfer; check id type.
  5. Root cause: Ordering only covers account-account locks. The callback acquires auditLock while an account lock is held, whereas audit takes auditLock then an account: a different order, so a cycle exists. A self-transfer breaks assumptions of two distinct locks.
  6. Fix: Short-term: call the listener after releasing the account locks (collect events, publish outside); reject self-transfers. Long-term: add auditLock to the global rank order (below accounts) or drop it for a lock-free queue.
List<Event> ev;
synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { ev = apply(from, to, amt); } }
ev.forEach(listener::onChange);         // no lock held
  1. Prevention: Written lock-rank table; lockdep-style test tooling; rule: no callbacks under a lock.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use one global lock now unless throughput allows; keep fine-grained locks but fix the rules.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just tryLock? -> Works as a fallback but needs back-off and retry limits.
  • What if the listener must be synchronous? -> Run it in the same order or make the audit sink lock-free.
  • Why mention Integer ==? -> Boxed ids compare by reference outside -128..127, breaking the order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A service had ordered locks documented on a wiki; a new "audit" feature added a lock the wiki never mentioned.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes ordering is complete.
  • Hire: finds the callback inversion and self-transfer.
  • Strong hire: publishes events outside locks, ranks every lock, adds an automated check.

questions.contextHtml:
After a flash-sale launch, 1.3% of checkouts fail with ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction (MySQL InnoDB). Traffic is 800 checkouts/s. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS:

*** (1) TRANSACTION: UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku=8812
*** (1) WAITING FOR THIS LOCK TO BE GRANTED: index PRIMARY of table `shop`.`stock` rec lock
*** (2) TRANSACTION: UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku=4410
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)

Each checkout updates stock rows for up to 6 items in cart order; the cart UI lets users add items in any order. CPU on the DB is 55%.
questions.promptHtml: Why are deadlocks happening, and how do you drive them to near zero?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn off deadlock detection" or "retry forever". Neither fixes the cycle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Isolation level? Does the transaction hold locks while calling a payment API? Are the sku lookups indexed? Does the app retry on 1213?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make sure the app retries the whole transaction with jitter; raise nothing else.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) rows locked in different orders by concurrent checkouts; (b) long transactions holding locks across external calls; (c) missing index causing wide or gap locks; (d) a hot row (one sku) pile-up; (e) detection cost (red herring: CPU is 55%).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare lock orders in the two reported transactions; EXPLAIN on updates; information_schema.innodb_trx; log transaction duration.
  5. Root cause: T1 locks sku A then B; T2 locks B then A. Classic opposite-order cycle, amplified by a hot-item surge.
  6. Fix: Short-term: sort items by sku inside the transaction before updating; keep the transaction to the stock updates only (no payment call inside). Add retry (3 attempts, jitter). Long-term: for ultra-hot SKUs use a conditional update WHERE qty > 0 and queue/serialise per sku.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 4410 AND qty > 0;   -- sorted by sku ascending
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 8812 AND qty > 0;
COMMIT;
  1. Prevention: Metric on 1213 rate; test that fires concurrent opposite-order checkouts; code review check for update ordering.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop isolation just to hide deadlocks, nor disable detection with hot rows without lowering innodb_lock_wait_timeout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if detection is saturating CPU on one hot row? -> Consider innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF with a low lock wait timeout, or serialise that sku.
  • Pessimistic vs optimistic? -> Optimistic versioning avoids long locks if conflicts are rare; hot SKUs conflict a lot.
  • Is retrying idempotent? -> Yes if the whole transaction restarts and external effects happen after commit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The deadlock rate fell from 1.3% to 0.02% after one line sorted items by id; the remaining cases were hot-sku contention and handled by a per-sku queue.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables detection or just increases timeouts.
  • Hire: orders updates and adds retries.
  • Strong hire: shortens transactions, uses conditional updates, handles hot rows, adds observability.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing API using a fixed pool of 10 threads (Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) hangs every Friday at peak. Health checks time out, CPU is 3%, no locks are held in the usual sense. Kubernetes restarts the pod after 3 failed probes and it recovers for a day.

$ jstack 2310 | grep -c "pool-1-thread"   -> 10
$ jstack 2310 | grep -A4 "pool-1-thread-3"
 java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
   at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(FutureTask.java:191)
   at com.shop.PriceService.compute(PriceService.java:57)

A recent change made compute() fan out three sub-requests to the same executor and wait for all.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What do you do about the restarts?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the pool to 50." Moves the threshold; a bigger burst re-creates it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the executor shared between request handling and subtasks? Queue bounded? When did fan-out ship? Any downstream slowness at the time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before restart capture a thread dump; temporarily raise pool size or disable fan-out via flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pool starvation: all 10 workers wait for subtasks queued behind them; (b) slow downstream holding workers; (c) real lock deadlock (ruled out by dump: no BLOCKED); (d) GC (CPU 3%, no).
  4. How I'd verify each: All pool threads in FutureTask.get, queue length >0 (ThreadPoolExecutor metrics); subtask stack frames absent.
  5. Root cause: Parent tasks occupy all threads while waiting for children that need a thread. It is a deadlock between tasks, not locks: Coffman holds (threads are exclusive resources, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular dependency through the queue).
  6. Fix: Short-term: separate executors for parents and children, or run sub-requests on a different pool. Long-term: async composition (CompletableFuture, coroutines) so no thread blocks, or ForkJoinPool where waiting threads help.
ExecutorService parents = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
ExecutorService children = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(30);
  1. Prevention: Metric on pool active/queue size; test with pool size 1; lint rule against blocking get() on the same executor; liveness probe that captures a thread dump.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just restart on probe failure without a dump; that hides the bug. More threads cost memory and context switching.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does it only hit at peak? -> It needs all 10 workers busy with parents at once.
  • Can a bounded queue help? -> It converts the hang into rejections, which at least surface.
  • Does virtual-thread / coroutine style fix it? -> It removes the thread scarcity, provided you do not pin or block on a bounded resource.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A retry-heavy service hit this in a minute-long outage; the postmortem fix was a dedicated pool for fan-out and a "pool size 1" test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises thread count or restarts.
  • Hire: identifies starvation and separates pools.
  • Strong hire: ties to Coffman, adds pool metrics and pool-size-1 tests, saves a dump before restarts.

questions.contextHtml:
A router service holds an in-memory routing table of 200k entries. 400k lookups/s across 32 threads (each lookup about 0.3 microseconds), updates arrive 5 times per second (rebuild of a few entries, ~2 ms). The team used ReentrantReadWriteLock. Observations: throughput saturates at 1.1M lookups/s total instead of expected 10M+; occasionally an update takes 800 ms to start.

perf: 42% of cycles in ReentrantReadWriteLock$Sync.tryAcquireShared (cmpxchg)

Another developer added code that takes the read lock, finds a stale entry and then calls writeLock().lock() to update it.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the symptoms and choose a better design. What about the read-to-write upgrade?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "RW locks are for read-heavy, so it should be fast." Ignores that readers still write the lock word and the starvation policy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must lookups see the update immediately? How large is the table (copy cost)? Is it fair mode? Do lookups hold the lock for the whole request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the upgrade path (it deadlocks); lower update rate or batch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) readLock() is an atomic update on one shared cache line, so 32 cores bounce it; (b) writers wait for a continuous stream of readers (starvation under readers-preference, 800 ms delay); (c) upgrade deadlock when two threads hold read locks and both want write; (d) table too large for copy-on-write (check).
  4. How I'd verify each: perf shows time in tryAcquireShared; jstack for threads holding read lock and waiting for write; measure wait time for the write lock.
  5. Root cause: The RW lock is itself shared state: each read acquisition is an atomic RMW (50 to 200 ns on contended cores), 100x the 0.3 us work in some cases. Writers can starve. Upgrade deadlocks because the writer waits for all readers including itself.
  6. Fix: Short-term: swap for a volatile immutable snapshot (copy-on-write): readers do one volatile load; the writer builds the new table and publishes it.
private volatile Map<String, Route> table = Map.of();
Route lookup(String k) { return table.get(k); }              // no lock
synchronized void update(Delta d) { var n = new HashMap<>(table); d.apply(n); table = Map.copyOf(n); }

At 200k entries a full copy is ~10 ms and 5 updates/s is affordable, or use persistent/structural sharing maps. Long-term: RCU-style or sharded tables. For upgrade: release read, take write, re-validate. 7. Prevention: Benchmark readers at full thread count; code review rule "never upgrade"; update-latency SLO. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Copy-on-write costs memory (2x briefly) and write latency; readers may see slightly old data for ms. I would not use StampedLock without a team that understands it, though optimistic reads help.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if updates rise to 500/s? -> Copying becomes costly; shard by key and copy per shard, or ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Can the writer be starved with COW? -> No; writers never wait for readers.
  • What about memory reclamation in C++? -> RCU or epoch-based reclamation; shared_ptr swap with atomics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A routing team's RW lock was replaced by a snapshot swap; lookups went from 1M to 14M/s on the same box and tail latency vanished.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps the RW lock and tweaks fairness.
  • Hire: moves to snapshot/COW and avoids upgrade.
  • Strong hire: explains lock-word cache-line bouncing, quantifies copy cost, discusses RCU and staleness trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A Python 3 + C extension service (multi-threaded, 16 threads) shells out to an image tool using os.fork() followed by exec in Python code, but a legacy C helper in the same process calls fork() and then does snprintf/malloc in the child before execve. About once per 20,000 calls the child hangs forever; the parent waits on waitpid and request threads pile up. The child's stack:

$ gdb -p 9731 -batch -ex "bt"
#0  __lll_lock_wait_private ()
#1  malloc ()
#2  child_setup () at helper.c:58
#3  spawn_tool () at helper.c:44

No other thread exists in the child.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the child stuck on a lock nobody holds, and how do you fix it without removing the feature?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "malloc is slow" or "add a timeout to waitpid". Doesn't explain the lock owner.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the parent multi-threaded at the fork moment (yes, 16)? What does the child do before exec? Which libc? Can we use posix_spawn?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a kill timeout around waitpid; reap and retry; limit concurrent spawns.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) another parent thread held malloc's arena lock at the instant of fork; (b) the child inherits a copy of the held lock but the holder thread does not exist; (c) a signal handler issue; (d) resource exhaustion (red herring: low load).
  4. How I'd verify each: The child backtrace shows __lll_lock_wait_private in malloc; the child has one thread; reproduce with a stress test that hammers malloc in other threads while forking.
  5. Root cause: fork() copies only the calling thread. If another thread was inside malloc (holding a lock), the child sees that lock held forever, because the owner thread was not copied. Calling non-async-signal-safe functions after fork in a multithreaded process is undefined.
  6. Fix: Short-term: only call async-signal-safe functions between fork and exec (dup2, close, execve), move the allocation before fork. Better: posix_spawn, or Python subprocess (uses vfork/posix_spawn). Alternative: pthread_atfork handlers to lock and unlock the mutexes around fork.
posix_spawn(&pid, "/usr/bin/tool", &file_actions, &attr, argv, environ);
  1. Prevention: Static analysis for fork-then-allocate; chaos stress with concurrent malloc and fork; wrapper that forbids raw fork.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: pthread_atfork is fragile (libraries, ordering). I would not add sleeps or retries as a fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is it rare? -> The fork must land during the tiny window another thread holds the arena lock.
  • Does exec right after fork avoid it? -> Yes, if nothing between needs locks.
  • Python multiprocessing "fork" start method? -> Same hazard; use spawn or forkserver with threads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A worker pool hung one child per week; the team took a month to see that the missing lock owner was a thread that no longer existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: timeouts only.
  • Hire: explains only the calling thread survives fork, uses exec or posix_spawn.
  • Strong hire: lists async-signal-safe rules, atfork limits, reproduction by stress.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review of a 41-minute outage. Services: Orders calls Inventory (sync), Inventory calls Pricing, and a recent change made Pricing call Orders to check bundle eligibility. Client timeouts are 30 s everywhere with 3 retries. Timeline: 14:02 deploy; 14:05 p99 ramps; 14:09 all three services show 100% worker threads busy, CPU 5%; 14:12 autoscaler adds pods, no effect; 14:20 error rate 78%; 14:43 rollback restores service.

Orders: pool active 200/200, queue 4,100   Inventory: 200/200   Pricing: 200/200
traces: Orders -> Inventory -> Pricing -> Orders -> ... (depth 3, repeated)
questions.promptHtml: What happened, why did scaling and retries make it worse, and what should change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network issue" or "add more pods". Misses the cyclic dependency and retry amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the Pricing change flagged? Any circuit breakers? What do retries do (immediate or backed off)? Are thread pools shared across endpoints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the Pricing change (done at 14:43; should be earlier); shed load at the edge; lower retries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) distributed deadlock: each service's workers wait on the next in a cycle; (b) retry storm (3x amplification at each hop yields up to 27x); (c) downstream database slowness (traces show waiting on RPC, not DB); (d) autoscaling (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace graph reveals the cycle; thread dumps show workers parked in HTTP client waits; compare request rate vs completions.
  5. Root cause: A cycle in the synchronous call graph with finite worker pools: when concurrency reaches the pool size, every worker waits for a callee that needs a worker in the original service. Timeouts of 30 s mean workers stay held; retries refill the queue; autoscaling adds pods but each pool saturates immediately (metastable failure).
  6. Fix: Short-term: break the cycle (move bundle eligibility into a local cache or event), set timeouts decreasing down the chain (Orders 10 s > Inventory 6 s > Pricing 3 s), retry only at the edge with budgets and jitter, add circuit breakers and bulkheads (semaphore per downstream). Long-term: dependency-graph linting in CI and architecture review for cycles.
  7. Prevention: Call-graph cycle detection from traces; load test with fault injection; concurrency limits with fast-fail; alert on pool saturation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply raise pool sizes; it delays the cliff and raises memory. Dropping retries entirely hurts transient failures; use budgets.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did scaling not help? -> The cycle consumes every added worker too; the constraint is the dependency, not capacity.
  • How would async I/O change it? -> No thread held, but queues and memory still grow; timeouts and limits still needed.
  • How to find cycles before shipping? -> Contract tests, service-graph analysis, dependency allowlists.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A postmortem concluded "an innocent feature call created a loop"; the real learning was that no one owned the global call graph.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network/traffic and scales.
  • Hire: identifies cycle and fixes via rollback plus timeouts.
  • Strong hire: explains retry amplification, decreasing timeouts, bulkheads, metastable failure and CI checks.

questions.contextHtml: An ingestion service accepts events (1 KB each) into an in-memory LinkedBlockingQueue with no bound, drained by 8 workers writing to a database. Normal: 3,000 events/s in, 3,000 out. A partner integration will raise peaks to 30,000 events/s for 10 minutes at a time, workers can sustain 5,000/s per instance. Heap is 4 GB.
questions.promptHtml: What happens at the peak, and how would you redesign the buffering, including shutdown and what to do when it is full?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the heap" or "add workers"; no bound, no policy, ignores DB limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can events be dropped, delayed, or must be durable? Is the producer a client who can retry? What is the DB write ceiling? Is order important? What is the peak shape and duration?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a size limit and return 429/503 with Retry-After at the edge; scale workers only if the DB can take it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) queue grows 25,000/s (30,000 in minus 5,000 out) = 25 MB/s, 15 GB over 10 minutes, so OOM in about 160 s; (b) GC thrash before OOM, latency collapse; (c) DB saturation if workers increase; (d) loss on crash since the queue is in memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Queue depth metric, heap graph and GC logs in a staging load test at 30k/s; DB write capacity test.
  5. Root cause: Producers outrun consumers with no back-pressure; an unbounded buffer converts overload into memory death.
  6. Fix: Use a bounded queue sized to burst tolerance, e.g. 30 s at the rate difference of 5,000/s = 150k events (~150 MB) hidden behind a policy: block the producer (back-pressure) for internal callers, reject with 429 for external, or spill to durable log (Kafka) when full.
BlockingQueue<Event> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(150_000);
if (!q.offer(e, 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { metrics.rejected.inc(); throw new Overloaded(); }
// shutdown: stop accepting, enqueue one POISON per worker, join

For 10-minute peaks (15 GB of backlog) the correct design is a durable log (Kafka) between ingest and DB writers, and scale writers horizontally to the DB's limit. 7. Prevention: Alert on queue depth over 50% and on rejects; load tests of the full peak; capacity doc listing DB limits. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Blocking producers propagates latency upstream; dropping loses data; spilling adds a dependency. I would not hide overload with a bigger heap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you choose the bound? -> Peak burst length x rate difference, capped by memory and acceptable latency (Little's law: depth / out-rate = delay).
  • What if order matters? -> Partition by key; one queue per partition.
  • How do consumers exit cleanly? -> Poison pill or channel close, then drain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "infinite" queue masked a slow database for weeks; the first partner spike took the host out in under three minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap or workers.
  • Hire: bounds the queue, applies back-pressure or shedding.
  • Strong hire: computes growth and delay, picks durable buffering for long peaks, handles shutdown and observability.
